lessons.title: What Is Anthropic and Claude?
lessons.description: Who Anthropic is, how the Claude model family is organised, and the difference between Claude.ai and the Claude API.

content.text: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company. Its assistant is called **Claude**. Developers can use Claude in two main ways: the consumer and team apps (Claude.ai, desktop and mobile apps) and the **Claude API** for building your own products.
The model family

Claude comes as a family of models at different points on the trade-off between capability, speed and cost. Larger, more capable models are better for hard reasoning and coding. Smaller, faster models suit high-volume work such as classification, extraction and quick replies. New versions are released regularly and older ones are retired on a published schedule, so never hard-code a model name without a plan to update it.
Choosing a model

items: Write 20 or more real test cases for your task.
Run them on a smaller model first.
Move up to a larger model only for cases that fail.
Compare quality, latency and cost, then decide per feature, not per product.

content.text: Claude.ai versus the API

items: **Claude.ai**: a chat product with its own features, usage plans and settings. Good for you using Claude.
**Claude API**: a programmable service you call from code and pay for by usage (tokens). Good for putting Claude inside your product.

content.text: A subscription to Claude.ai does not include API credits. API usage is billed separately through the Anthropic Console.
What you will need

items: An Anthropic Console account and an API key.
Node.js 18 or later.
A way to keep secrets out of your code, such as environment variables.

content.text: Model names, features and limits change. Always check the current Anthropic documentation (docs.anthropic.com) for the latest model identifiers, parameters and pricing before you ship.

faqs.q: Is the Claude API free?
faqs.a: API usage is paid by tokens. Check the Anthropic Console and pricing page for current terms, including any free credits.

faqs.q: Which Claude model should I pick?
faqs.a: Test your own examples. Start with a smaller, faster model and move up only where quality is not good enough.

lessons.keywords: what is claude, anthropic claude models, claude api vs claude.ai

lessons.title: Set Up the Claude API in Node.js
lessons.description: Create an API key, store it safely, install the SDK and send your first request.

content.text: This lesson takes you from zero to a working request.
1. Get an API key
Create an account in the Anthropic Console, add billing or credits, and create an API key. Copy it once; you cannot view it again later.
2. Keep the key secret

items: Put it in an environment variable called ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, never in source code or the browser.
Add .env to .gitignore.
Call Claude only from your server. A key in front-end code can be stolen and used on your bill.
Use separate keys for development and production, and rotate a key if it leaks.

content.text:
npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk
echo "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key-here" >> .env
3. Send your first message
The reply is a message object. Its **content** is a list of blocks (usually one text block), and **usage** reports how many input and output tokens you used.
Model names, features and limits change. Always check the current Anthropic documentation (docs.anthropic.com) for the latest model identifiers, parameters and pricing before you ship.

faqs.q: Can I call the Claude API directly from React?
faqs.a: No. Anyone could read your key in the browser. Call it from your server and let the front end talk to your server.

faqs.q: What if I get an authentication error?
faqs.a: Check that the key is correct, that the environment variable is loaded where the code runs, and that your account has credits.

lessons.keywords: claude api node.js, anthropic sdk setup, claude api key, first claude request

lessons.title: Claude API Tokens, Pricing and Rate Limits
lessons.description: How tokens are counted and billed, how to estimate and track cost, and how rate limits work.

content.text: Every request is billed by the tokens it uses. Understanding tokens saves money and prevents surprises.
Input and output tokens

items: **Input tokens**: your system prompt, the conversation history, documents and tool definitions.
**Output tokens**: what Claude writes back. They usually cost more per token than input.

content.text: You set **max_tokens** to cap the length of the reply. It is a hard ceiling, not a target.
Count before you send
Track usage and cost

items: Log the usage numbers from every response with the feature name and user id.
Convert tokens to cost using the current price list, and show it on an admin dashboard.
Set a per-user or per-day quota so one user cannot run up your bill.

content.text: Rate limits and errors

The API limits how many requests and tokens you can use per minute. If you exceed a limit you get a 429 error. Retry with **exponential backoff** (wait 1 second, then 2, then 4, with a little randomness), and add a timeout so a stuck call does not hang your server. The official SDK already retries some errors for you.
Ways to cut cost

items: Use the smallest model that passes your tests.
Keep prompts short and remove unneeded history.
Use prompt caching for repeated text (lesson on advanced features).
Use the batch API for work that can wait.

content.text: Model names, features and limits change. Always check the current Anthropic documentation (docs.anthropic.com) for the latest model identifiers, parameters and pricing before you ship.

faqs.q: Why was my bill higher than expected?
faqs.a: Common causes are long conversation history sent on every call, large documents, very long outputs and retries. Log token usage per request to find out.

faqs.q: What does a 429 error mean?
faqs.a: You hit a rate limit. Wait and retry with backoff, and consider queueing requests.

lessons.keywords: claude api pricing, token counting, rate limits 429, reduce llm cost

lessons.title: The Messages API Explained
lessons.description: System prompts, user and assistant messages, multi-turn chat and the most useful request parameters.

content.text: The **Messages API** is the core of Claude's API. You send a list of messages and get the next assistant message back.
The request
Parts of the request

items: **model**: which Claude model to use.
**max_tokens**: required. Upper limit for the reply.
**system**: instructions and persona that apply to the whole conversation. It is a separate field, not a message.
**messages**: alternating user and assistant messages. The first one must be from the user.
**temperature** and other sampling settings, where the model supports them: lower for consistent output.
**stop_sequences**: strings that end the reply when produced.

content.text: Multi-turn conversations
Claude does not remember earlier requests. To continue a chat you send the whole history every time: add the assistant's last reply and the new user message to the array.
Because the history grows, long chats cost more and can hit the context limit. Summarise or trim old turns.
Reading the response

items: **content**: list of blocks (text, and later tool calls).
**stop_reason**: why it stopped, for example the model finished or hit max_tokens.
**usage**: input and output token counts.

content.text: Always check stop_reason. If it says the limit was reached, the answer was cut off.
Model names, features and limits change. Always check the current Anthropic documentation (docs.anthropic.com) for the latest model identifiers, parameters and pricing before you ship.

faqs.q: Does Claude remember my previous API calls?
faqs.a: No. Each call is independent. You must send the conversation history with every request.

faqs.q: Where do I put instructions, system or user message?
faqs.a: Put stable rules and persona in the system prompt and the changing request and data in the user message.

lessons.keywords: claude messages api, system prompt claude, multi-turn conversation api, max_tokens

lessons.title: Streaming Claude Responses to the Browser
lessons.description: Show text as it is generated using streaming, with a Node.js and Server-Sent Events example.

content.text: Waiting ten seconds for a full answer feels slow. **Streaming** sends the text as it is generated, so users see words appear almost at once.
Streaming with the SDK
Passing the stream to a web page
Use **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**: a simple one-way stream from server to browser. In Express you set the right headers and write each chunk.
Things to get right

items: Handle errors that happen part-way through a stream.
Cancel the request when the user closes the page, so you stop paying for tokens nobody reads.
Do not buffer: reverse proxies such as nginx may need buffering turned off for the streaming route.
Still validate any final structured result once the stream ends.

content.text: Model names, features and limits change. Always check the current Anthropic documentation (docs.anthropic.com) for the latest model identifiers, parameters and pricing before you ship.

faqs.q: Does streaming make the answer cheaper?
faqs.a: No, the token cost is the same. It only improves how fast the first words appear.

faqs.q: Why does my streamed response arrive all at once?
faqs.a: A proxy or compression layer is probably buffering it. Turn off buffering for that route.

lessons.keywords: claude streaming, server-sent events express, stream llm response node

lessons.title: Error Handling, Retries and Timeouts
lessons.description: Build a reliable Claude integration: handle API errors, rate limits, overload and timeouts safely.

content.text: Production AI features fail in boring ways: rate limits, network blips, slow responses. A few habits keep them from becoming user-facing outages.
Know the error types

items: **400-level request errors**: your request is invalid (bad parameter, too many tokens). Retrying will not help; fix the request.
**401 or 403**: key or permission problem.
**429**: rate limited. Retry later.
**500-level or overloaded**: a temporary service problem. Retry with backoff.

content.text: Retry the right things
Timeouts and cancellation
Set a sensible timeout and make long calls cancellable. If the user leaves, abort the request.
Degrade gracefully

items: Show a clear message when AI is unavailable, and let the user continue without it.
Fall back to a secondary model or provider for critical features.
Use a circuit breaker: after repeated failures stop calling for a short time instead of piling on.
Log the error, request id and token usage so you can debug later.

content.text: Never put the raw error text from the API in front of your users. It can include details they should not see.

faqs.q: Should I retry a 400 error?
faqs.a: No. A 400 means the request itself is wrong, so fix it instead of retrying.

faqs.q: What is exponential backoff?
faqs.a: Waiting longer after each failed attempt (for example 1s, 2s, 4s), usually with a bit of randomness, so you do not overload the service.

lessons.keywords: claude api errors, retry exponential backoff, rate limit handling, llm reliability

lessons.title: Prompt Caching and Batch Processing
lessons.description: Cut cost and latency for repeated prompts with prompt caching, and use batches for work that can wait.

content.text: Two features can reduce what you pay when you send a lot of similar requests.
Prompt caching

If many requests begin with the same long text, such as a detailed system prompt, a policy document or a set of examples, you can mark that part for **caching**. Later requests that start with the same text can reuse it at a lower cost and often with lower latency.

items: Put the **stable** content first and the changing user content last. Caching matches a prefix.
Cached content expires after a short time if it is not reused, so it helps most for busy features.
There are minimum sizes and exact pricing rules; read the current docs.

content.text: Batch processing

The **Message Batches API** lets you submit many requests together and collect results later, usually at a lower price than real-time calls. It suits overnight jobs such as scoring thousands of stored resumes or generating descriptions in bulk. It does not suit anything a user is waiting for.
Which to use

items: Same long prefix, many live requests: prompt caching.
Many independent jobs, no rush: batch.
Both can be combined.

content.text: Model names, features and limits change. Always check the current Anthropic documentation (docs.anthropic.com) for the latest model identifiers, parameters and pricing before you ship.

faqs.q: Where should cached text go in the prompt?
faqs.a: At the start. The cache works on a matching beginning of the prompt, so put the part that never changes first.

faqs.q: Can users wait for a batch result?
faqs.a: Not usually. Batches finish within a window, not instantly, so use them for background work.

lessons.keywords: claude prompt caching, message batches api, reduce claude cost

lessons.title: Images, PDFs and Documents with Claude
lessons.description: Send images and PDFs to Claude for reading, extraction and summarising, with practical limits and privacy notes.

content.text: Claude can read images and PDFs, not only plain text. That opens up tasks such as extracting details from a scanned certificate, reading a table in a PDF or checking the layout of a resume screenshot.
Sending a PDF
Images work the same way with an image block and a media type such as image/png or image/jpeg.
Good uses

items: Resume and invoice parsing.
Reading tables and forms.
Describing charts and screenshots.
Comparing two documents.

content.text: Things to watch

items: Documents and images count toward your input tokens, so large files cost more.
There are limits on file size and page count. Check the docs.
Scanned or low-quality files can be misread. Validate extracted data.
These files often contain personal data. Tell users what you do with them, do not store them longer than needed and never log them in plain text.

content.text: Model names, features and limits change. Always check the current Anthropic documentation (docs.anthropic.com) for the latest model identifiers, parameters and pricing before you ship.

faqs.q: Can Claude read scanned PDFs?
faqs.a: It can often read text in images, but quality depends on the scan. Always validate extracted data for important uses.

faqs.q: Is it safe to upload resumes to the API?
faqs.a: Treat them as personal data: minimise what you send, protect them in transit and storage, follow your privacy policy and check the provider's data-retention terms.

lessons.keywords: claude pdf api, claude vision, document extraction llm, resume parsing ai

lessons.title: Claude Tool Use: How It Works
lessons.description: How Claude calls your functions: tool definitions, the request and result loop, and what your code must do.

content.text: A language model cannot browse your database or send an email by itself. **Tool use** (also called function calling) lets you describe functions to Claude. Claude decides when one is needed and asks **your code** to run it. Claude never runs the function itself.
The flow

items: You send the user message plus a list of tool definitions.
Claude replies with a **tool_use** block: the tool name and the arguments it wants.
Your code checks the request, runs the function and gets a result.
You send the result back as a **tool_result**.
Claude uses the result to write the final answer, or asks for another tool.

content.text: Define a tool
The **description** is the most important part. It is how Claude decides when to use the tool, so say what it does and when to use it.
Run the loop
Put a cap on the number of loop turns so a confused model cannot loop forever and run up cost.
Model names, features and limits change. Always check the current Anthropic documentation (docs.anthropic.com) for the latest model identifiers, parameters and pricing before you ship.

faqs.q: Does Claude execute my function?
faqs.a: No. Claude returns the tool name and arguments, and your code decides whether and how to run it.

faqs.q: Can Claude call several tools at once?
faqs.a: Yes, a reply can contain several tool_use blocks. Return one tool_result for each, matched by tool_use_id.

lessons.keywords: claude tool use, function calling claude, tool_use tool_result, anthropic tools node

lessons.title: Designing Safe Tools and Permission Checks
lessons.description: Write tool schemas that work well, validate arguments, add human approval and defend tools against misuse.

content.text: Tools turn a chat model into something that can change real data. That makes safety your job, not the model's.
Design tools Claude can use well

items: One clear job per tool, with a precise name such as search_jobs rather than do_job_stuff.
Describe parameters in plain language and give allowed values with enum.
Return small, useful results, not raw database dumps.
Return clear error messages so Claude can recover or tell the user.

content.text: Validate everything

Model-generated arguments are untrusted input, like form data from a stranger. Validate types and ranges, check that the user is allowed to do the action, and never build database queries by pasting strings.
Permissions and approval

items: Give each tool only the access it needs (least privilege).
Ask the person to confirm sensitive actions: delete, send, pay, publish.
Make actions **idempotent** where you can, so a repeated call does not do the harm twice.
Log every tool call with who, what and when.

content.text: Untrusted tool output

Results can contain text from outside, such as a web page or an email. Treat it as data. It may contain instructions aimed at the model (prompt injection), so never let tool output grant new permissions.
Test your tools
Build a set of example requests and expected tool calls, and check that Claude chooses the right tool, with the right arguments, and refuses when it should.

faqs.q: Why must I validate tool arguments?
faqs.a: Because the model can produce wrong or manipulated values. Validation and ownership checks stop it affecting data it should not.

faqs.q: Which actions need human approval?
faqs.a: Anything hard to undo or with real-world effects: deleting data, sending messages, payments, publishing.

lessons.keywords: tool use security, llm function calling safety, prompt injection tools, human in the loop

lessons.title: Project: Resume and Job Matching with Claude
lessons.description: Put it together: a Node.js endpoint that scores how well a resume fits a job, with structured output and validation.

content.text: In this project you build an endpoint that takes a resume and a job description and returns a structured match report. It uses ideas from this course: system prompt, structured output through a tool, validation and error handling.
1. Define the output as a tool
Instead of asking for JSON in text, force Claude to fill a schema by giving it one tool and requiring its use.
2. Call Claude
3. Validate and respond

items: Validate the report with Zod and clamp the score to 0-100.
Return only the fields you need.
Log token usage for cost tracking.
Add rate limits per user so the endpoint cannot be abused.

content.text: 4. Be honest in the UI

Present the result as guidance, not as how any particular employer's system will score the resume. You can compare your approach with our free [job description matcher](/resume-job-description-matcher) and [ATS checker](/features/ats-checker).
Next steps

items: Add a test set of 20 resume and job pairs and track score stability.
Cache the long rules prompt.
Add retrieval of example bullet points (see the RAG course).

faqs.q: Why use a tool for structured output?
faqs.a: Forcing a tool call makes Claude return arguments that follow your JSON Schema, which is more reliable than asking for JSON in plain text.

faqs.q: Can AI scores be trusted for hiring decisions?
faqs.a: Treat them as a helpful signal only. Keep a human in charge of any decision that affects a person.

lessons.keywords: claude project node.js, resume job match ai, structured output tool_choice

lessons.title: Prompt Design for Claude: XML Tags, Examples and Roles
lessons.description: Claude-friendly prompt habits: XML tags, separating instructions from data, examples and long-document prompting.

content.text: The general prompt-engineering rules apply to Claude, and a few habits fit it especially well.
Use XML tags to separate parts
Wrapping parts of the prompt in tags makes it clear what is an instruction and what is data. It also helps defend against injection, since you can say that anything inside a tag is content only.

<instructions>
Summarise the job post for a candidate in 3 bullet points. Plain English.
</instructions>

<job_post>
{{job_text}}
</job_post>
Be specific, say why

items: Give the goal and the reader: "for a daily-wage worker applying through their phone".
Explain the reason for a rule, because Claude follows rules better when it understands them.
Tell it what to do, not only what to avoid.

content.text: Examples
A few varied examples inside <example> tags set format and tone better than long descriptions.
Long documents

items: Place long documents near the top, then the question at the end.
Label documents (<document index="1">).
Ask Claude to quote the relevant passage first when accuracy matters, then answer.

content.text: Common task prompts

items: **Classification**: list the allowed labels and ask for one label only.
**Extraction**: give a schema, say what to do with missing values.
**Summarisation**: state length, audience and what to keep.
**Coding**: give the language, the existing code and tests that must pass.

content.text: Test and version
Keep prompts in files, version them and run them against a test set after each change, as in the prompt-testing lesson of the fundamentals course.

faqs.q: Are XML tags required for Claude?
faqs.a: No, but they are a clear, reliable way to separate instructions, data and examples, and many people find they improve results.

faqs.q: Where should I put the question in a long prompt?
faqs.a: After the documents. Putting the question at the end usually works better for long inputs.

lessons.keywords: claude prompt engineering, xml tags prompts, long document prompting, claude system prompt
